title: Computer Architecture Foundations
description: What a machine is optimizing, how instructions mean work, and why pipelines and caches exist before anyone says out-of-order.

sourceReferences.title: MIT 6.823 Computer System Architecture
sourceReferences.notes: ISA and caches/VM before ILP. Module quizzes, not micro-topic quizzes.

sourceReferences.title: Stanford CS149 Parallel Computing
sourceReferences.notes: Latency/throughput and data-parallel thinking before GPU vocabulary.

modules.title: What the machine is optimizing
modules.blurb: Latency, throughput, and why some work is wide.

modules.title: Instructions and execution
modules.blurb: ISA as a contract, not a brand.
learningObjectives: Walk one instruction through fetch and execute

modules.title: Keeping a sequential core busy
modules.blurb: Pipelines and the hazards that empty them.

modules.title: Locality before coherence
modules.blurb: Caches and virtual addresses as mechanisms.
learningObjectives: Use locality to explain a cache
Separate virtual addresses from physical lines

concepts.name: Latency versus throughput
concepts.summary: How long one thing takes versus how much work finishes per unit time.
objectives: Distinguish latency from throughput with a concrete pipeline or factory example
Explain why raising clock or width can move one without the other

concepts.name: Data-parallel work
concepts.summary: The same operation over many independent elements, versus one long dependent chain.
objectives: Recognize when a computation is data-parallel
Contrast that with a sequential dependence a GPU cannot wish away

concepts.name: Amdahl and the serial leftover
concepts.summary: Speedup is owned by the part you cannot parallelize.
objectives: State Amdahl's bound as the serial fraction that remains
Predict why speeding only the parallel part stops helping

concepts.name: CPI, IPC, and why clock is not the story
concepts.summary: Performance as work per time, factored into frequency and useful work per cycle.
objectives: Factor time into instruction count, CPI, and clock period
Explain why a higher clock can still lose performance

concepts.name: Instruction set architecture
concepts.summary: The programmer-visible contract: operations, registers, memory, and exceptions.
objectives: Separate ISA from a particular microarchitecture
Name what the ISA must specify for a program to be portable

concepts.name: Stored-program machine
concepts.summary: Instructions live in the same memory as data, with all the consequences.
objectives: Explain why instructions and data sharing one memory matters
Name the bottleneck that shared instruction/data memory creates

concepts.name: Fetch, decode, execute
concepts.summary: The sequential loop a pipeline will later overlap.
objectives: Walk one instruction through fetch, decode, and execute
Distinguish this sequential loop from a later pipeline

concepts.name: Datapath versus control
concepts.summary: Where the bits are transformed versus who decides the next transform.
objectives: Separate the datapath that transforms values from the control that sequences it
Say which part decides the next operation

concepts.name: Addressing modes
concepts.summary: How an instruction names the data it wants.
objectives: Identify how an instruction names its operands
Contrast register, immediate, and memory addressing

concepts.name: RISC and CISC as encoding bets
concepts.summary: Dense encodings versus regular pipelines — not a moral ranking.
objectives: Treat RISC and CISC as encoding and pipeline bets, not brands
Explain why dense encodings and regular pipelines trade

concepts.name: Endianness
concepts.summary: Byte order as a convention that becomes a bug when ignored.
objectives: Define endianness as the byte order of a multi-byte value
Predict a bug when two sides disagree on endianness

concepts.name: Exceptions and interrupts
concepts.summary: Leaving the instruction stream because the world, or the program, demanded it.
objectives: Distinguish a synchronous exception from an asynchronous interrupt
Explain why the machine must save enough state to resume

concepts.name: Memory-mapped I/O
concepts.summary: Devices that look like addresses.
objectives: Explain how a device register can be an ordinary address
Contrast MMIO with a separate I/O instruction space

concepts.name: Instruction pipelines
concepts.summary: Breaking instruction execution into overlapping stages.
objectives: Explain how overlap raises throughput without shrinking per-instruction latency
Name why a bubble exists

concepts.name: Pipeline hazards
concepts.summary: Data, control, and structural stalls that break ideal overlap.
objectives: Name the three hazard classes
Say what forwarding can and cannot fix

concepts.name: Result forwarding
concepts.summary: Bypassing the register file so a dependent instruction need not wait for writeback.
objectives: Say what forwarding bypasses
Predict when forwarding cannot help

concepts.name: Control hazards
concepts.summary: Not knowing the next PC until the branch resolves.
objectives: Explain why a branch makes the next PC unknown
Name the cost of guessing wrong

concepts.name: Instruction-level parallelism as slack
concepts.summary: Independent instructions nearby in one thread — the raw material of later OOO.
objectives: Define ILP as independent instructions in one thread
Contrast ILP with data-parallel work across elements

concepts.name: Temporal and spatial locality
concepts.summary: Why the next access is often near, or the same as, the last one.
objectives: Distinguish temporal from spatial locality
Use locality to explain why a small fast memory helps

concepts.name: The cache hierarchy
concepts.summary: L1/L2/L3 as a latency-capacity trade, not three unrelated boxes.
objectives: Explain L1/L2/L3 as a latency-capacity trade
Say why the closest cache is smallest

concepts.name: Hits, misses, and miss types
concepts.summary: Compulsory, capacity, and conflict — different failures, different fixes.
objectives: Name compulsory, capacity, and conflict misses
Match a miss type to a plausible fix

concepts.name: Write-through and write-back
concepts.summary: When a store dirties a line versus when it updates memory.
objectives: Contrast write-through with write-back
Explain dirty bits and write-allocate as consequences

concepts.name: Virtual addresses
concepts.summary: The names a process uses, mapped later onto physical lines.
objectives: Separate a process virtual address from a physical line
Explain why two processes can use the same virtual address

concepts.name: The TLB as a cache of translations
concepts.summary: A miss here is not a cache miss.
objectives: Describe the TLB as a cache of translations, not data
Distinguish a TLB miss from a data-cache miss

concepts.name: The memory wall
concepts.summary: Why processors started hiding latency instead of waiting honestly.
objectives: State the memory wall as processors outrunning DRAM latency
Explain why caches hide latency rather than deleting it
